linq.title: LINQ for Java · PiscesCup
linq.description: LINQ for Java: an Enumerable query library for Java 25, featuring fluent queries, deferred execution and primitive-specialized sequences.
linq.lead: Composable data processing for Java collections and sequences using a LINQ query style.
linq.overview: LINQ for Java provides queries for Java collections and sequences through the Enumerable model. Methods such as where, select and orderBy compose data processing steps; many intermediate operations use deferred execution and run when results are enumerated or consumed.
linq.enumerablesIntro: Object sequences and specialized int, long and double sequences provide query entry points for the corresponding data types.
linq.objectDescription: Create sequences from arrays, collections or varargs, then filter, order, group and join objects.
linq.intDescription: Use Linq.ofInts for int-specific queries and numeric aggregation such as sum and average.
linq.longDescription: Use Linq.ofLongs for long-valued data, reducing unnecessary boxing and unboxing in primitive pipelines.
linq.doubleDescription: Use Linq.ofDoubles for filtering, transforming and aggregating double-valued data.
linq.features.filterDescription: Filter elements with where, transform results with select, and control sequence ranges with skip and take.
linq.features.orderDescription: Combine orderBy and thenBy for multi-level sorting, and use groupBy to group elements by key.
linq.features.joinDescription: Correlate sequences with join and groupJoin; use distinct, union, intersect and except for deduplication and set operations.
linq.features.aggregateDescription: Consume results with operators such as count, first and aggregate, or materialize them as lists, arrays and maps.
linq.prepareDescription: The repository README and compiler configuration require JDK 25 or later.
linq.installDescription: Select a build tool and copy the dependency configuration example. Version 1.0.0 is taken from the repository's pom.xml; confirm publication or follow the README to build and install it in a local repository before use.
linq.sampleDescription: Filter even numbers, calculate their squares, and retrieve the query results with toArray.
linq.relatedDescription: Related projects include the Commons Lib utility dependency and the separate linq-in-java repository.

examples.heading: Code examples
examples.runHint: Expand an example to view its complete Java class and output. Configure the dependency, save the code with the displayed filename, and run the main method. After selecting a different dependency version, check its compatibility with the version used by the examples.
examples.source: View this example in the README
examples.commons.intro: This section presents five examples adapted from Quick Examples in the Commons Lib README, with main methods and output statements added. Compilation and output were verified with Commons Lib 1.1.6.
examples.commons.namingDescription: Use StringUtils to convert between snake_case, UpperCamel and lowerCamel naming styles.
examples.commons.intervalDescription: Create a closed-open [1, 10) interval with IntInterval and check its boundaries and formatted representation.
examples.commons.counterDescription: Create a counter with Counter.atomic, increment and add to it, then read its current value.
examples.commons.functionDescription: Calculate volume with TriFunction, using full invocation, partial application and memorized result caching.
examples.commons.pairDescription: Transform the left-hand string with mappedLeft while preserving the right-hand Integer value.
examples.linq.intro: This section presents six queries from the LINQ for Java README, with imports, main methods and required record definitions added. The examples were compiled and run against repository version 1.0.0 with JDK 25. Refer to the dependency section for publication status.
examples.linq.filterDescription: Create an Int sequence with Linq.ofInts, filter even numbers with where, and retrieve the results with toArray.
examples.linq.projectionDescription: Use select and String::length to map names to their string lengths and collect the results into a List.
examples.linq.orderingDescription: Apply multi-level sorting by age and then name. Person.toString retains the README output format; the optional annotation is omitted.
examples.linq.aggregationDescription: Calculate the sum and average with IntEnumerable's sum and average methods. The example corrects the README output label age to avg.
examples.linq.setsDescription: Use distinct, except, intersect and union for unique values, difference, intersection and union.
examples.linq.studentsDescription: Based on the README Student example, select students with scores of at least 80, order by descending score, and extract their names.

tutorial.home.title: Let's start making mods
tutorial.home.description: My Fabric modding process, written up as a tutorial. Start with environment setup in Chapter 00.
chapter00.intro: We won't add an item just yet. First we'll set up the tools, make IDEA comfortable to use, and get to know the project files. Once the template starts successfully, we'll have a solid place to write code.
chapter00.baseline: This chapter targets Minecraft 26.3, JDK 25 and IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3. Menu paths were checked against official material on 2026-11-05. Chinese labels are provided for the Simplified Chinese UI; language-pack wording may vary slightly. Search Settings for the English setting name if needed.
chapter00.environment.title: 1. Set up the development environment
chapter00.environment.jdkIntro: The JDK includes development tools such as javac as well as the Java runtime. Install JDK 25, rather than just a JRE. Having Java bundled with your game launcher doesn't mean IDEA and Gradle are already configured.
chapter00.environment.arch: Choose the operating system and architecture for your machine: typically x64 on a Windows PC and aarch64 on an Apple Silicon Mac. Open a new terminal after installation and check both commands below. Both should report version 25; the patch number doesn't need to match a screenshot.
chapter00.environment.jdkMismatch: If java and javac report different versions, check PATH and JAVA_HOME. JAVA_HOME should point to the JDK root directory, not its bin directory. Open another terminal after changing them.
chapter00.environment.idea: 1.2 IntelliJ IDEA: use JDK 25 for the project and Gradle
chapter00.environment.ideaIntro: Open the template project after installation. The project SDK and Gradle JVM are separate settings, so check both. Changing only the SDK can leave Gradle running on an older Java version.
chapter00.environment.ideaRuntime: The bundled JetBrains Runtime runs IDEA itself. You don't need to replace it to work on this mod. Configure the project SDK and Gradle JVM instead. On macOS, Settings is under the IntelliJ IDEA application menu; the settings categories are the same.
chapter00.environment.template: 1.3 Fabric Mod Template: generate a project that runs
chapter00.environment.generator: Open the official Fabric template generator
chapter00.environment.templateIntro: Select Minecraft 26.3 and fill in the mod name, mod ID and package name. The examples here use Vocabulary Spark and vocabulary-spark. Use your own package name, such as io.github.piscescup.vocabularyspark. The mod ID is also its resource namespace, so settle on it early.
chapter00.environment.templateOptions: Choose Java and the client-source and data-generation options that suit your project. Extract the download to a permanent folder, then use IDEA's Open action on the root containing settings.gradle, build.gradle and gradlew. Don't open only src. The first Gradle sync downloads dependencies, so give it time to finish.
chapter00.environment.firstRun: After the sync finishes, start the development client from a terminal in the project root. Use the first command in Windows PowerShell or the second on macOS/Linux. They are alternatives, not two consecutive steps.
chapter00.environment.success: This step is complete when the development client opens. If it fails, look for the first useful error in Build or the terminal and check the JDK and dependency sync. There's no need to change unfamiliar template settings at random.
chapter00.settings.title: 2. Everyday IDEA settings
chapter00.settings.intro: Follow the hierarchy shown in the Settings window. English paths retain the UI names, and Chinese paths are shown alongside them, so you don't need to change IDEA's language. Appearance is a matter of comfort; the JDK and encodings deserve closer attention.
chapter00.settings.shortcuts: Default shortcuts are Ctrl + Alt + S on Windows/Linux and ⌘ + , on macOS. Use the search field in Settings when a category is hard to find. Every path below starts from this window.
chapter00.settings.reopenBody: Enable this to reopen your last projects when IDEA starts. Clear it if you'd rather begin at the welcome screen. It changes startup behavior and doesn't remove any projects.
chapter00.settings.updatesBody: This stops automatic IDE update checks and notifications. It isn't an installation lock. Plugin updates have a separate option. If IDEA is managed by JetBrains Toolbox, turn off automatic tool updates in Toolbox Settings → Tools → Update all tools automatically; the IDE's update page mainly handles plugins in that setup.
chapter00.settings.themeBody: This changes the application windows and toolbars. Light or dark is fine—pick what stays comfortable over time. Code colors have a separate setting below.
chapter00.settings.uiFontBody: Enable the custom font and adjust its size. This affects text in menus and the project tree, rather than the Java code in the editor.
chapter00.settings.backgroundBody: Open a project first, choose an image and adjust its opacity. Select This project only to keep it local to that project. This is entirely optional; keep the code readable against the image.
chapter00.settings.editor: 2.4 Editor colors, font size and comments
chapter00.settings.schemeBody: This controls colors for syntax such as keywords, strings and comments. If IDEA asks you to duplicate or save a built-in scheme before editing it, make your own copy first.
chapter00.settings.codeFontBody: JetBrains Mono is a reasonable starting point; choose a size that works for you. If the change seems to do nothing, check Color Scheme → Color Scheme Font for a scheme-specific font overriding the default.
chapter00.settings.commentsBody: Select the element for line, block or documentation comments and change its foreground color. For Java-specific colors, look under Editor → Color Scheme → Java. Clear Inherit values from when the element inherits its defaults. The Chinese labels for individual comment types may vary with the language pack.
chapter00.settings.linesBody: Line numbers are useful when discussing errors: you can point to a specific line. Method separators are optional horizontal dividers that can make a long class easier to scan.
chapter00.settings.completionBody: In 2026.3, suggestion options are under Popup. Enable Show suggestions as you type. Adjust Match case to your preference. With the default Windows keymap, Ctrl + Space requests completion without waiting for a popup.
chapter00.settings.importBody: Enable Add unambiguous imports on the fly to import a class automatically when the choice is unambiguous. Optimize imports on the fly cleans up unused or disordered imports; whether to enable it is up to you.
chapter00.settings.importReminder: Still check the package name. Different Minecraft versions and libraries can contain similarly named types. Match the package used by the example. IDEA needs your choice when more than one candidate fits.
chapter00.settings.encodingBody: Set all three to UTF-8, then check the file and directory overrides for older encodings. Project Encoding applies to the current project. To adjust defaults for future projects, use File → New Projects Setup → Settings for New Projects.
chapter00.settings.encodingConvert: If an existing file is already garbled, don't immediately save after changing this setting. Identify its original encoding and use the encoding menu in the status bar to Reload or Convert as appropriate. Transparent native-to-ascii conversion handles Properties escapes; it isn't the UTF-8 switch.
chapter00.settings.consoleBody: This controls how IDEA decodes console output. It doesn't change the bytes written by Java or another tool. If logs are still garbled, check the producer's encoding too. Console encoding is separate from source-file encoding.
chapter00.settings.header: 2.10 A header for new Java classes
chapter00.settings.headerBody: Put the following in the file-header template, using your own author name. REN YuanTong and 1.0.0 are kept here to match the example. ${NAME} is an IDEA template variable, not text to leave unchanged in the generated Java source.
chapter00.settings.headerScope: Choose Default for IDE-level templates or Project for the current project's templates. Under Files → Class, check for #parse("File Header.java"). It's usually present already, so don't add it twice. The change affects files created afterwards, not existing classes.
chapter00.plugins.title: 3. IDEA development plugins
chapter00.plugins.intro: Get the basic project running before adding plugins. The following two are useful options, but they don't replace the JDK, Fabric Loader or the project's dependencies.
chapter00.plugins.mcdevBody: Adds Minecraft-aware inspections and navigation. Install a version compatible with IDEA 2026.3 and restart if requested. We'll still create the project with Fabric's official generator, since plugin templates can lag behind a new game version.
chapter00.plugins.ignoreBody: Useful if you often edit .gitignore files. The generated template already includes one, which is a good starting point. Git's ignore rules work even without this plugin.
chapter00.plugins.language: Want a Chinese UI? Use the bundled language support
chapter00.plugins.languageBody: Current IDEA includes Chinese language support. You don't need to follow older tutorials that install a separate pack. If Chinese isn't listed, check that Chinese Language Pack is enabled under Plugins → Installed, then restart if requested.
chapter00.files.title: 4. Get to know the project files
chapter00.files.intro: You don't need to memorize every file on the first day. Start with two roles: Gradle controls how the project is built, while Fabric's configuration tells the game how to load the mod. The descriptions below follow the 26.3 template.
chapter00.files.gradle: 4.1 Gradle: the build and its dependencies
chapter00.files.gradleRow0: The build script declares Loom, Minecraft, Fabric Loader/API, compilation and resource processing. The 26.3 template uses net.fabricmc.fabric-loom; don't copy older plugin names and modImplementation snippets unchanged.
chapter00.files.gradleRow1: Stores versions and project properties. The current template uses keys such as minecraft_version, loader_version, fabric_api_version, version and group. Older names such as mod_version and maven_group may not match this script.
chapter00.files.gradleRow2: Defines the project name and plugin-resolution repositories. Understand its role before changing it; the template doesn't need arbitrary repository changes to run.
chapter00.files.gradleRow3: Pins the Gradle distribution used by this project. Use its wrapper rather than installing a separate global Gradle.
chapter00.files.gradleRow4: Gradle Wrapper launchers: gradlew for macOS/Linux and gradlew.bat for Windows.
chapter00.files.gradleRow5: Local Gradle state and build output. These aren't the source directories, and generated build files generally don't belong in source control.
chapter00.files.fabric: 4.2 Fabric: entrypoints, resources and mod metadata
chapter00.files.fabricRow0: Common Java code, including the ModInitializer entrypoint. It may run on the client and a dedicated server, so keep client-only rendering types out of common code.
chapter00.files.fabricRow1: Client-only code when split source sets are enabled, usually including ClientModInitializer. Its presence depends on the generator options.
chapter00.files.fabricRow2: Describes the mod. Start with id, name, version, environment, entrypoints, depends and mixins. After renaming or moving an entrypoint class, check its fully qualified name here.
chapter00.files.fabricRow3: The namespaced client-resource directory, under resources, for translations, textures and similar assets. vocabulary-spark must match the mod ID.
chapter00.files.fabricRow4: Namespaced server data, such as recipes and loot tables. Add subdirectories as the mod needs them rather than creating every possible directory now.
chapter00.files.fabricRow5: Lists mixin classes and related options. Client mixin configuration may live under src/client/resources. For now, knowing where the configuration lives is enough.
chapter00.files.fabricRow6: A possible output directory when data generation is enabled and configured; it's not guaranteed in every base template. Update the generators and regenerate instead of treating it as hand-written source.
chapter00.files.idReminder: Keep the mod ID and Java package name separate. vocabulary-spark is a valid mod ID, but a Java package segment cannot contain a hyphen. You might use vocabularyspark in the package while keeping vocabulary-spark for resources.
chapter00.files.buildBody: Look for outputs in build/libs afterwards. It may also contain source or other supplementary JARs, so distinguish the mod artifact from a sources JAR. Verify the untouched project runs and builds before changing it; that gives you a useful baseline.
chapter00.habits.title: 5. My habits: a References class
chapter00.habits.intro: I like to keep the mod ID, metadata, logger and shared helpers in a References class. Fabric doesn't require this structure; it just gives these values one predictable home. In a small project, keeping them in the entrypoint is fine too.
chapter00.habits.exampleIntro: The example includes explicit imports, uses Gson and Log4j, and adds a private constructor to prevent instantiation. Add the package declaration used by your project, and keep the class name, mod ID and fabric.mod.json ID aligned.
chapter00.habits.row0: The unique mod ID and resource namespace. Define it once rather than repeating the literal throughout the project.
chapter00.habits.row1: The Fabric Loader instance, used to query discovered mod information.
chapter00.habits.row2: The ModContainer found by ID. orElseThrow() deliberately fails when it isn't found, making an inconsistent ID something to fix immediately.
chapter00.habits.row3: Provides metadata. MOD_NAME and MOD_VERSION come from it rather than duplicating the name and version elsewhere.
chapter00.habits.row4: A shared JSON serializer. setPrettyPrinting() makes output readable. disableHtmlEscaping() leaves some HTML characters unescaped; it doesn't make JSON safe to insert as HTML.
chapter00.habits.row5: A Log4j logger named after the mod. Import the Log4j Logger type here, not org.slf4j.Logger.
chapter00.habits.row6: Adds the mod's namespace without repeating MOD_ID. Pass only the path, without a vocabulary-spark: prefix.

chapter00.habits.lifecycle: 5.3 Understand initialization before using it everywhere
chapter00.habits.lifecycleBody: The metadata fields execute in order when the class is first initialized. Even a call to fromPath() initializes the class and queries its ModContainer first. Use it once Fabric's mod metadata is available, rather than trying it in a standalone main() without Fabric.
chapter00.habits.constant: MOD_ID is a compile-time String constant, so reading it alone generally doesn't initialize the class. MOD_NAME and MOD_VERSION are runtime fields. If you later want a fully independent ID helper, separate fromPath() from metadata lookup.
chapter00.habits.annotationsBody: Here @NonNull explicitly means org.jspecify.annotations.NonNull, and @Contract comes from org.jetbrains.annotations.Contract. NonNull describes a non-null return type, while "_ -> new" describes a fresh object on normal return. They describe contracts rather than performing runtime checks. When importing them, avoid Lombok’s similarly named annotation.
chapter00.habits.versionBody: This example uses net.minecraft.resources.Identifier and fromNamespaceAndPath as in the MC 26.3 template. Don't substitute old net.minecraft.util.Identifier or ResourceLocation imports. The official template uses SLF4J; keeping Log4j here is an explicit project choice, not a requirement for Fabric mods.
chapter00.finish.title: A good place to pause
chapter00.finish.body: Make sure the template runs, Gradle builds and encodings agree before moving on. You don't need to memorize the References class. Come back to the relevant part when you need resource IDs, logging or configuration files.
